## Why a Population Study?

The individual posts ([Diaw](../diaw-35bpm/index.qmd), [Stockton](../stockton-durability/index.qmd)) establish signals in curated cohorts. The population study is the credibility check: does the gap persist when the reference class is every high-workload guard or forward in the BRef era, not a hand-selected 15?

It also surfaces unexpected outliers — players whose durability is unusual in ways the curated analysis did not anticipate.

---

## Cohort Definition

**Candidates scraped:** 1,995 players from BRef player index (A–Z), all positions, debuts 1980–2010.
**Currently fetched:** 108 players (87 population + 21 PG/PF cohort). Full fetch would cover ~1,500+ eligible players but requires several hours of wall time due to BRef rate limits.

The analysis below runs on the 108 available players. Percentile ranks are therefore provisional — they reflect placement within the current data, not the full BRef era. Directional findings (Stockton/Diaw near the durable extreme) are unlikely to reverse as coverage expands; absolute percentile values will shift as more players are added.

**Era variable:** `era = f"{(debut_year // 10) * 10}s"` — used as a fixed covariate to control for era-level pace and usage differences (1980s, 1990s, 2000s).

---

## E1: Career Durability Distribution

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-e1-pop
#| fig-cap: "Career games missed per 82 — 108-player population (partial A-section). Stockton and Diaw labeled."
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of games missed per 82-game season for the 108-player population. Stockton sits at the far left (1.18), Diaw near the low end (4.93)."
from IPython.display import Image
p = DATA_DIR / "figures/population/e1_histogram.png"
if p.exists():
    display(Image(filename=str(p)))
```

Among the 108 players in the current data, Stockton's 1.18 games missed per 82 places him at the 0.9th percentile — effectively the floor of the distribution. Diaw's 4.93 sits at the 5.6th percentile. Both findings are provisional on the partial population, but the distribution is right-skewed (most players miss substantially more games than Stockton), and the low end is dominated by long-career players with unusually intact availability records.

**Selection note:** population conditioned on all fetched players, not a ≥ 600 game filter. Players with very short careers inflate the high-miss-rate tail (see Outlier Table below). The population E1 estimand is therefore placement *within the full distribution of fetched players*, not within the long-career subset.

---

## Outlier Table

The table shows the 10 most and 10 least durable players in the current 108-player population:

| Player | Seasons | Active Games | Games Missed/82 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| John Stockton | 19 | 1,504 | 1.18 |
| Gary Payton | 17 | 1,335 | 1.63 |
| Thurl Bailey | 11 | 847 | 2.36 |
| Mark Jackson | 17 | 1,296 | 4.03 |
| Gene Banks | 5 | 388 | 4.40 |
| Boris Diaw | 14 | 1,064 | 4.93 |
| Derek Harper | 16 | 1,199 | 5.19 |
| Terry Porter | 17 | 1,274 | 5.30 |
| Danny Ainge | 13 | 989 | 5.92 |
| Jerome Allen | 1 | 76 | 6.00 |

Note that the bottom 10 (highest games missed/82) are dominated by players with 1–2 season careers — Blake Ahearn (78.1), Joe Alexander (74.0), Miloš Babić (73.0), etc. These are not legitimate comparators; they played too few games for the statistic to be meaningful. The 600-game threshold applied in the cohort analyses exists precisely to exclude this artifact.

## E3: Shot Selection B2B vs Rest

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-e3-pop
#| fig-cap: "E3: shot selection on B2Bs vs rest — 108-player population. Each point is a player; Stockton and cohort players visible."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter of B2B minus rest differences in 3PA/FGA (x-axis) and FTA/FGA (y-axis) for the 108-player population."
p = DATA_DIR / "figures/population/e3_scatter.png"
if p.exists():
    display(Image(filename=str(p)))
```

Stockton's B2B shot-selection pattern (Δ3PA/FGA = +0.002, ΔFTA/FGA = −0.049) sits in the lower-right quadrant: essentially flat three-point rate, largest FTA/FGA decline in the cohort. In the broader 108-player population, the FTA/FGA decline on B2B nights is common — the population median is slightly negative — so Stockton's position reflects the magnitude (d = −1.62 in the PG cohort) rather than uniqueness of direction. Diaw's pattern (+0.007 3PA/FGA, −0.033 FTA/FGA) also appears in the lower-right, slightly less extreme.

---

## What the Data Can and Cannot Say

The population study inherits all selection caveats from the individual posts. Additional notes:

- **Era confound:** earlier decades had different pace, usage, and medical practices. The era fixed effect controls for mean differences but not heterogeneity within eras.
- **Position coding:** BRef position labels are inconsistent across eras. Forwards and guards with dual-position codes are assigned to their primary listed position.
- **Incomplete population:** the population scrape covers BRef index pages as of the fetch date. Players whose careers predate BRef's digital records (pre-1980) are excluded by construction.

---

## Conclusion

With 108 players fetched from the BRef era (partial A-section of a ~1,995-candidate index), Stockton sits at the 0.9th percentile of games missed per 82 — effectively the most durable player in the available data. Diaw sits at the 5.6th percentile. Both figures are provisional on partial coverage: as the population expands toward the full 1,995-candidate index, absolute percentile values will shift. The directional finding — both players near the durable extreme of a right-skewed distribution — is robust to additional data.

The population study answers the cherry-picking objection to the individual analyses: Stockton and Diaw were not selected because they happen to look good in a small cohort. They stand out in the broader distribution of fetched players, across positions and eras, using the same E1 metric. What remains to be established at scale is whether the full 1,500+ player population changes the picture materially — a fetch that requires several hours of BRef rate-limited requests and is deferred to a future update of this post.

The bottom of the E1 distribution is uninformative: short-career players (1–2 seasons) with very high games-missed-per-82 are a data artifact, not legitimate comparators. The 600-game threshold from the cohort analyses exists precisely to exclude this tail. Applying that threshold to the population would require fetching enough players to make the filtered N meaningful — a task that depends on completing the full population fetch.
